abstractText:
Global climate change has generated significant fluctuations in ambient growth temperature, which profoundly influences diverse developmental, physiological, and morphological responses in plants, including rapid stem and root elongation, enhanced leafstalk growth and upward leaf bending, and early flowering. Understanding how plants adjust their developmental programs in response to temperature variations is central to improve plant fitness and sustain crop productivity. Most temperature signaling mechanisms were revealed at the whole-plant level, which averages distinct organ and cell types and thus inadvertently creates a one-size-fits-all illusion of proposed thermal sensing and response mechanisms. The proposed experiments are aimed at developing a novel miniature device to study thermal sensing and responses at the organ and cell levels. This new technology allows accurate induction and monitoring of thermal changes in a specific organ, tissue, or cell, making it possible to differentiate distinct thermal responses in various organs and cell types, and unveil the communication mechanisms between different organs and cell layers during coordinated thermal responses. The technology, not yet developed so is potentially risky in execution, is expected to be high reward because it will revolutionize research on thermal sensing and responses in various multicellular organisms and unicellular colonials. This knowledge can be used to advance our understanding of how global warming affects plant growth and development and provide the knowledge basis that may facilitate scientists to generate climate-smart crops. The project also offers opportunities in interdisciplinary research training for students of underrepresented groups.

The investigators of this collaborative project plan to use thermoresponsive hypocotyl (the embryonic stem) and root growth in the dicotyledonous plant Arabidopsis thaliana as a model to establish the Miniature heater-assisted thermomorphogenetic study (Miheats). The project comprises three components. First, a novel manufacturing technique will be developed to produce low-cost, self-designed miniature heaters that are scalable, durable, and flexible. Next, Miheats will be implemented in planta and a series of phenotypic and genetic analyses of Arabidopsis seedlings will be performed to evaluate the technical outcomes of Miheats. Finally, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses will be employed to identify co-regulated gene and protein modules in different organs/cells and unveil the homogeneity and heterogeneity of organ- and cell-specific thermomorphogenetic signaling. Therefore, the project addresses Understanding the Rules of Life and grows Convergence Research by infusing advances in micro/nanofabrication and minimally invasive approaches to create a new solver for investigating organ/cell-autonomous and -nonautonomous reactions as well as interorgan and intercellular communications in response to temperature fluctuations in multi-cellular organisms. Further, this high risk / high reward project will improve the Vision and Change in Undergraduate Biology Education core competencies, especially the ability to tap into the interdisciplinary nature of science and the ability to communicate and collaborate with other disciplines, of underrepresented minority students at the University of Mississippi.

projectOutComesReport:
The objective of this research was to develop scalable, low-cost, and flexible microheaters and to apply them in plant thermal studies to reveal the molecular mechanisms by which plants sense and respond to high temperatures.

In this project, we fabricated two types of heaters for biological applications. We developed a stable printing process to fabricate a wired microheater with a resolution of 100 µm that can be applied directly to a plant leaf. This microheater can maintain 47°C for more than 2 hours and 27°C for 24 hours. After applying the heater to plant leaves, we detected a systemic signal arising from local treatment of organs (e.g., embryonic leaves), demonstrating the microheater’s capability for studying plant responses to high temperatures. We observed that local heat treatment on one organ (e.g., a leaf) could induce transcriptomic changes in distal organs (e.g., other leaves or the stem). We also designed and developed a low-cost, centimeter-scale heating device for confocal microscopic applications. By integrating this device into microscope slides, we performed live-cell imaging of plants during heat treatment and captured dynamic subcellular events, such as the assembly of heat-induced stress granules.

We also developed a high-throughput, ultrasonic-assisted, clog-free electrohydrodynamic (EHD) printing process for highly viscous, fast-drying inks, achieving unsurpassed resolution. Traditional EHD and other nozzle-based printing techniques often suffer nozzle clogging when using inks with high viscosity, high solid loading, and/or rapid drying rates. Such clogging leads to unstable printing. Because EHD printing is a high-resolution technique, this instability significantly compromises print quality and increases defects. We successfully designed and integrated both electric and acoustic fields into one printhead. This innovative design generates internal ink circulation, preventing water loss and sedimentation—two primary causes of nozzle clogging. We validated the performance of this vibration-assisted printhead with polyethylene oxide (PEO) ink and demonstrated its capability by fabricating high-resolution 2-D patterns. With this printhead, we extended stable printing times from 10 seconds to over 3 minutes. Furthermore, it achieves 1 µm resolution at a stable printing speed of 30 mm/s. This development overcomes long-standing nozzle-clogging issues and offers great potential for the mass fabrication of micro-devices such as microheaters and microactuators.

This project also investigated the direct printing of 3-D microarrays for biosensing. Traditional MEMS (micro-electromechanical systems) technologies enable the fabrication of high-density, high-resolution 3-D arrays. However, process limitations make it difficult to manufacture 3-D arrays with varying pitches and shank sizes. We developed a high-resolution 3-D printing process for molten metal that fabricates 3-D arrays with different shank and pitch sizes in a single step. This process provides a new solution for fabricating 3-D sensors designed for spatial sensing.

In addition, we explored the use of machine learning with internal and external datasets to study relationships among material parameters, printing parameters, and printing behaviors. The resulting model predicts feature size and printing behavior with accuracy greater than 95%. This model guides material selection, testing, and process control, reducing time and cost when fabricating microreactors.

Project outcomes were shared broadly: (1) a TEDx University of Mississippi talk for the community; (2) presentations at technical conferences, including SME’s North America Manufacturing Research Conference (NAMRC) in 2023 and 2024, the Plant Biology 2024 meeting, and the 34th International Conference on Arabidopsis Research (ICAR 2024); (3) incorporation into coursework for undergraduate and graduate students in ME 523 Introduction to Additive Manufacturing, ENGR 546 Micro/Nanoscale Fabrication, BISC 516 Plant Physiology, and BISC 580 Plant Biotechnology; and (4) publication of five papers in leading journals and one book chapter. Several undergraduate and graduate students were mentored through this project, training future scientists in plant biotechnology and engineers in additive manufacturing. The project also offered hands-on research opportunities to high-school scholars recruited through the ARISE summer research program at the University of Mississippi.

abstractText:
Material properties are often linked to the atomic structure and chemistry of its internal interfaces. Among the internal interfaces, heterointerfaces are boundaries separating two materials with different atomic structure and chemistry. The atomic structure and chemistry of these heterointerfaces are complex and cannot be easily predicted from the individual materials that form the heterointerface. This complexity increases exponentially in multi-component heterointerfaces as it involves a vast number of chemical possibilities at the interface. Thus, designing the chemistry of a novel multi-component heterointerface with a targeted material property is a challenging task. This research project aims to enhance our current capability to determine the chemistry of a multi-component heterointerface with a targeted electronic property for photovoltaic applications using a combination of electronic structure calculations and machine learning approach. Machine learning tools can substantially reduce the time needed to identify the chemistry of a heterointerface that meets a desired electronic property need by efficiently extracting hidden chemistry-property relationships, a key factor toward accelerated discovery of novel heterointerface. The proposed project addresses the important federal government mandate of Materials Genome Initiative, the objective of which was to substantially reduce the time and cost to discover, manufacture, and deploy advanced materials.

Multicomponent heterointerfaces have long intrigued materials scientists and physicists, in part, because of the sheer complexity of their atomic and electronic structure and chemistry. Such complexity can make designing a novel multi-component heterointerface with a targeted material property a non-trivial task. This is because navigating the vast combinatorial chemical and configurational possibilities between multiple elements at the interface is simply too large. This research project aims to design the chemical composition of a heterointerface for photovoltaic application with a targeted electronic property using a combination of electronic structure calculations and machine learning approach. More specially, the PI plans (a) to develop an in-depth understanding of the underlying physics that determines the electronic and atomic structure of the heterointerface using electronic structure calculations; and (b) to apply machine learning tools to explore hidden chemistry-property relationships of the interface, to predict the chemistry of the heterointerface for a desired electronic property. The proposed approach is a departure from the traditional time-consuming and expensive Edisonian trial-and-error approach of synthesis-testing experimental cycles; thus, it can substantially accelerate materials discovery. The PI anticipates that upon completion of this project a generic computational template to investigate structure-chemistry-property relationship of highly complex multi-component heterointerfaces will be generated.  Finally, machine learning will be an integral part of future materials discovery. The knowledge gained from this project will help train student(s) on machine learning tools and their utility in materials research, increasing their exposure early in their careers to this growing and influential materials science field.

This study investigates how one localized segment of an advantaged group understands its position in the societal context in an era in which general views of that position may be changing.  Theory and past research suggest that people’s ideas are influenced by the major social, political, and economic events through which they live, and that people’s sense-making tends to vary by region and locality.  In this research, members of the target group are interviewed to investigate their understandings of their position and their associated thought processes.  Findings from this project will help to develop a more nuanced view of the regional group studied, and in particular will aid those designing practices to mitigate undesirable effects of differences in opportunities.  Honors undergraduate students will assist in data collection, helping to build the methodological skills of the next generation of scientists.

Data for this project come from in-depth interviews of 150 members of the advantaged group, divided between two locations: one moderately sized city and one town.  Sampling follows a purposive design to maximize the range of interviewees’ contexts and relevant experiences.  Data are analyzed using flexible coding and standard software for analyzing interview and qualitative data.  This project is jointly funded by the Sociology Program and the Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR).

projectOutComesReport:
With generous support from the National Science Foundation, I was able to hire, teach, and train a total of five graduate students in how to design social research, how to conduct in-depth qualitative interviews, how to code that interview data, and how to prepare that data for dissemination.

I want to stress that because I work in a department with only an MA-granting graduate degree program, all five students were or are Masters students. Yet, we were incredibly successful, as I’ll describe below.

In addition to teaching and training graduate students, funding from this project allowed me to align one of my undergraduate seminars and the students enrolled in it with my team’s research efforts. Those undergraduate students – around 12 total – were also trained in how to design social research, and allowed to accompany my graduate student team members on several interviews. Some, after preparation, were even allowed to serve as ‘second interviewers’, giving them hands-on research experiences as undergraduate students.

Funding for this project allowed us to make significant intellectual contributions to the sociological understanding of the relationship between race and region; how a person’s racial identity is tied, concretely, to the kinds of places where they live, work, and get along in life. We presented four papers across two separate conferences from this project. We published one manuscript from this project in the very highly regarded journal, Social Problems. Funding from this award allowed us to publish this article open-access, so that anyone can read and make use of our research. We have a second manuscript that has been accepted for publication in an edited volume, forthcoming with Polity Press, an academic publishing company based in the UK.

I want to stress that these publications involved MA-level students. The first publication, in Social Problems, includes four of those graduate students as co-authors. For MA-level students, this is unprecedented. The second publication includes two of those graduate students as co-authors. So, in sum, four of the graduate students funded through this project have one publication of record; two of the graduate students have two publications of record.

Finally, the broader impacts from this project are directly connected to its intellectual impact. A major aim of this project was to provide greater access and opportunities for underrepresented students into STEM fields and career pathways. All five graduate students aligned with this project are women. Two of the five women are members of minoritized groups. Three of the five women are first-generation college students. All five of these women have now had opportunities to present this work at professional conferences they otherwise may not have been able to attend; and four of the five students have had the opportunity to learn how to prepare this work for publication, including earning co-authorship.

I am incredibly thankful for the generous support the National Science Foundation has provided me for this research. And, it’s not done! Already, I am planning the next phases of this research project, envisioning how to expand upon it and include even more students as research partners and collaborators.

abstractText:
For over a century, researchers have studied Einstein's theory of general relativity (GR) -- our best understanding of gravity -- with increasing sophistication and precision.  With direct detections of gravitational waves (GWs) from Advanced LIGO and Virgo, it is now possible to test GR in the fully nonlinear, dynamical, strong-field regime when black holes (BHs) merge with each other.  Gravitational-wave detection also opens the possibility to observe more subtle aspects of GR, like the permanent deformation to spacetime ("memory") after a GW passes.  Both these new tests and the subtle effects of memory require higher precision predictions and more careful calculations than before.  Specifically, to carry out precision tests of GR requires performing supercomputer simulations of merging BHs, both in GR and in theories beyond GR. One aspect of improving the precision of tests of GR is gaining a deeper understanding of subtle effects in GR simulations, such as the fundamental coordinate freedom in GR, that makes it more difficult to compare between independent simulations.  Part I of the research component of this award is to better understand these GR subtleties.  As for simulations beyond GR, the PI and collaborators have developed a technique for classes of theories that are "close" to GR, but these simulations have not yet been advanced to the level of sophistication of GR simulations.  Part II of the research component of this award will advance the state of the art of beyond-GR simulations.  Simultaneously and independently, the educational component of this award will support development of interactive visualization to help educators teach GR and GWs to a broader audience.  These interactive tools will be made available online to reach beyond classroom education.

Part I of the research component consists of studies intending to push numerical relativity waveforms to higher precision, not by improving resolution or simulation methods, but rather by capturing a number of subtle effects.  These studies include: (i) high-precision multi-mode quasinormal ringdown fits, especially for precessing systems, with the goal of ultimately building a ringdown surrogate model; (ii) developing a framework for comparing waveforms after modeling out by transformations of the Bondi–Van der Burg–Metzner–Sachs (BMS) group, for apples-to-apples comparisons between simulations performed in different gauges, and for better hybridization with post-Newtonian or effective-one-body waveforms; (iii) statistically validating BMS (non-)conservation laws; and (iv) explaining the existence of an approximate symmetry of outgoing radiation from quasi-circular binary inspirals.  Part II of the research component focuses on advancing the state-of-the-art in simulating binary BH mergers beyond-GR theories of gravity.  This program includes: (i) bringing generation of beyond-GR waveforms into "production" mode; (ii) controlling the growth of secular effects (due to using perturbation theory) by applying the numerical dynamical renormalization group; (iii) building a surrogate model for beyond-GR waveforms; and (iv) validating this machinery by applying it to scalar-tensor theory, which can also be treated without recourse to perturbation theory.  Finally, the educational component involves producing interactive visualizations to help teach the principles of GR and GW physics.  These interactive visualizations will include particles orbiting around BHs, how GWs deform spacetime, how GWs get projected onto LIGO antenna patterns, and even how GWs from a BBH change as the intrinsic and extrinsic parameters are varied.

This award is jointly supported by the Major Research Instrumentation, the Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR), and the Chemistry Research Instrumentation programs. The University of Mississippi is acquiring a Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) imaging microscope to support the research of Professor James Cizdziel and colleagues Carolyn Freiwald, Vijayasankar Raman, Courtney Roper, and Matteo D'Alessio. This instrument facilitates research in the areas of chemistry, energy, materials, biomedical and pharmaceutical sciences, as well as archeology and anthropology. In general, Fourier-Transform Infrared Spectroscopy measures the intensity of the absorbed or transmitted infrared radiation when it passes through a solid, liquid or gaseous sample. The resulting spectra represent the molecular absorption or transmission of the tested substance. When infrared radiation passes through a compound part of it is absorbed by the constituent molecules which vibrate or rotate at certain frequencies. In a heterogeneous sample this powerful analytical tool is good for identifying chemical composition qualitatively. The information can also be used to create an image of the material composition in a sample. This instrument enhances the educational, research, and teaching efforts of students at all levels in many departments as well as provides accessibility for use at nearby institutions.

The award of the FTIR imaging microscope is aimed at enhancing research and education at all levels, especially in areas such as environmental and forensic chemistry involving microplastics, atmospheric fine particulates and metabolized drugs. Research in the area of archeology and anthropology is also facilitated by identifying compounds in prehistoric paints and analyzing Mesoamerican artifacts. Studies focused on biomedical and pharmaceutical sciences for studying serum exposed ionic liquids, the role of the active human IGF-1 protein in alterations of ischemic tissues, topical drugs and dietary supplements are also pursued as are those focused on analysis of materials relevant for aerogels, water treatment and solar cells.

The University of Mississippi (UM) acquired a new automated Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) microscope for research and education. The instrument, called LUMOS II, combines optical (light) microscopy with IR spectroscopy. Spectroscopy is the interaction of radiation (light) with matter, and light in the infrared range induces many molecules to vibrate as distinct frequencies. The LUMOS II measures absorption of IR light producing a vibrational fingerprint (spectrum) of the sample and yielding a wealth of information on molecular structure, surface characteristics, and the spatial distribution of chemicals in samples, with little to no sample preparation or method development.

In the two years since its installation, the LUMOS II has been integrated into three different courses from three different departments at UM, used by at least twenty undergraduate and graduate students in the course of their original research and training, and integrated into a successful summer research programs, including an NSF Research Experience for Undergraduates (REU) physical chemistry program and a McNair Scholars program. At least a dozen research groups from UM and Rhodes College have used the instrument to advance research streams in environmental and forensic chemistry, biomedical and pharmaceutical science, archeology and anthropology, and material science. Moreover, the instrument is believed to have helped UM in the recruitment and retention of high-quality students.  

Outcomes include at least thirteen peer-reviewed papers which have been published in high-quality scientific journals. Briefly, research outcomes include: a better understanding of the abundance, characteristics, and sources of microplastic pollution in the Mississippi River system, in oysters from Gulf Coast, and in a wastewater treatment plant; the advancement of ionic liquids for transdermal transport and drug delivery; evaluation of the distribution of chemical markers in stroke-damaged tissues; new methods in chemical imaging of trace evidence in forensic investigations and in the study of paint binders in prehistoric rock pictographs.

New analytical methods were developed to determine the size, shape, and composition of the small plastic particles in different environmental matrices and in biological tissues, including oysters. Oysters serve as an important economic resource to the region and provide many ecosystem benefits, but as filter feeders, they are susceptible to microplastic pollution. The work enabled using the LUMOS II provided much needed empirical data on the abundances and sizes of MPs in oysters from the Mississippi Sound, as well as the tissues where they reside. Further, using the LUMOS II, researchers obtained data needed to (1) help understand risks posed by microplastics, (2) guide policy makers to improve air and water quality, and (3) improve people’s education around microplastic pollution. Use of the instrument has also led to a potential economical approach to mitigate microplastic (and other) pollution in both agricultural and urban stormwater runoff using biochar.

Examining the spatiotemporal characteristics of microplastics in a wastewater treatment plant, researchers demonstrated that flow rates and treatment times can profoundly influence microplastic concentrations in the treated effluent, and that the optimal wastewater treatment conditions also yield the best microplastic removal efficiency.

In other work, researchers used the instrument to obtain FTIR spectra of tire wear particles (TWPs) providing much-needed empirical data on airborne TWPs along roads with different traffic characteristics. This work showed the effects of traffic volume, speed, and driving behavior on the levels of airborne TWPs.

The instrument was also used in a study of the impact of water on choline-2-octenoic ionic liquid-facilitated transdermal transport which showed that it is critical to comprehensively consider interactions between IL components, co-solvents, and drug molecules when formulating ILs for transdermal transport applications.

Chemical imaging with the LUMOS II helped indicate that neuronal and astrocytic IGF-1 signaling influences stroke damage but IGF-1 signaling within these individual cell types is not required for minimizing tissue damage or behavioral outcome.  

Overall, the instrument has been popular with students and faculty alike as a new tool for basic and applied research, and in research training of undergraduate and graduate students. The instrument is particularly well-suited to identify sample constituents and map the distribution of chemicals in-situ in a variety of materials, and has thus been used to advance research in multiple scientific areas.

abstractText:
With the support of the Chemical Catalysis program in the Division of Chemistry, Elizabeth T. Papish of The University of Alabama, Jared H. Delcamp of The University of Mississippi, and Charles Edwin Webster of Mississippi State University will study the transformation of the greenhouse gas carbon dioxide into synthetic fuels with new metal catalysts of novel structure. Envisioning a sunlight-driven energy infrastructure in our future requires efficient and robust catalysts that can power artificial photochemically driven reactions for fuel production. Using sunlight to create fuels as stored chemical energy available on demand is attractive relative to our current fossil fuel-reliant infrastructure. Nonetheless, this vision requires fast, durable, and selective catalysts that would ideally utilize readily available and affordable metals where feasible. The current lack of such catalysts represents a significant gap in the current knowledge base. The investigators will design new catalysts for carbon dioxide reduction to fuels with innovative structures previously untested. They will work on controlling and understanding carbon dioxide reduction through design of robust and highly active catalysts via synthetic, mechanistic, and computational studies. These studies can elucidate the factors that impact catalysis and eventually lead to the production of solar fuels from a greenhouse gas in a carbon neutral fashion. The results of this research are to be shared broadly, and this project is expected to help train a diverse group of 10-15 undergraduate and graduate students over the project period. The investigators will visit local schools for outreach events and host high school students in their research laboratories. In addition, undergraduate students will perform catalytic reactions in a teaching lab setting, and the results will be shared with the community, to offer educational experiences along with experiment verification.

With the support of the Chemical Catalysis program in the Division of Chemistry, Professor Elizabeth T. Papish of The University of Alabama, and her collaborators, Jared H. Delcamp of The University of Mississippi, and Charles Edwin Webster of Mississippi State University, will study carbon dioxide reduction with new metal catalysts containing first row transition metals and macrocyclic ligands. More efficient, robust, and selective catalysts are needed for artificial photochemical schemes aimed at converting carbon dioxide to fuels or fuel precursors. Using prior experience in the synthesis and testing of efficient self-sensitized catalysts that retain activity in water, the collaborative team will work on designing new robust catalysts using two strategies: active site isolation via use of a macrocyclic pincer ligand, and low-coordinate metal complexes via the use of low-valent metals. Synthetic, mechanistic, and computational studies will be directed toward three goals: (1) to increase the understanding of CNC-pincer ligated first-row metal catalysts, (2) to expand the knowledge of under-explored supramolecular catalysts with iridium photosensitizers, and (3) to understand the behavior of homogeneous catalysts linked to semiconductor electrodes. The long-term goal is to move the field of molecular catalyst design closer to a durable, earth-abundant metal-based catalyst system for the photocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide coupled to water splitting in a solar powered photo-electrochemical cell using the knowledge gained in the above tasks. Applying these ideas systematically to first-row metals is still largely uncharted territory, with the potential payoff being understanding how to make solar fuels with first row-metal complexes. The scientific results will be communicated through publications, presentations, and patents; the broader impacts will include outreach events and catalysis research experiments in an undergraduate teaching laboratory setting.

projectOutComesReport:
The project has lead to significant advancement in intellectual merit with respect to catalyst design for the conversion of carbon dioxide to a more readily used carbon product through the use of sunlight. This work focused on the design of catalysts using more abundant and affordable metals rather than the traditionally used precious metals that have limited supply and high prices. This project resulted in the identification of abundant metal based catalysts using periodic table first row transition metals based on nickel, iron, and cobalt rather than commonly employed second and third row metals like rhenium, platinum, and ruthenium. It has been a long standing challenge to use metals like nickel with sunlight due to these metals rapidly converting sunlight to heat rather than allowing time for chemical reactions to occur. Through careful catalyst design, we have found multiple systems that use these first row affordable metals to drive the conversion of carbon dioxide to either carbon monoxide or formate with sunlight. Both products can readily be used in making synthetic gasoline or used directly as a fuel via combustion or in an electrochemical cell to produce electric. 

Broader impacts results from this project include putting forward the catalyst design approaches that can be used by multiple fields. As an example, sunlight or light driven catalyst has become increasingly important in pharmaceutical manufacturing through processes such as photoredox catalysis. These approaches allow for the access of new reaction transformations for faster drug synthesis at lower temperatures and pressures than many traditional routes resulting in significant savings in drug development, manufacturing, and availability. Additionally, this work is of broad interest to the photophysics community where there are very few examples of a first row metal approach working well with photodriven processes. Additionally, three students were trained in a highly technical area with an undergraduate continue to a top graduate school for further education, a graduate student entering an American industrial position which strengthens our workforce in a highly technical area, and a graduate student joining the US Patent Office to assist in evaluating highly technical data.

abstractText:
L-functions have played a pivotal role in the modern development of number theory and they can be used to study a wide variety of problems. The tools used to study L-functions draw from many branches of mathematics including analysis, algebra, algebraic geometry, representation theory, and mathematical physics while number theory has important applications outside of mathematics to fields such as theoretical computer science and cryptography. Many of the topics investigated in this project concern the distribution of zeros of L-functions and related topics in arithmetic. This relationship is central to two of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, the Riemann hypothesis and the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture. The investigator will continue training and mentoring graduate students in this research area, and this project will provide research training opportunities for them. 
 
One of the problems in this project will investigate a thin family of Dirichlet L-functions which experimentally has significant and previously undetected bias in distribution of the gaps between their zeros. This bias seems to have an arithmetic explanation that corresponds to the non-vanishing of a certain Gauss type sum connected to moments of these L-functions. Other problems study the distribution of zeros and moments of the Riemann zeta-function, the prototypical example of an L-function, giving insight on previously unexplained, and in some cases previously unobserved, phenomena. The investigator also intends to combine tools from Fourier analysis with the theory of L-functions to study prime geodesics and to give improvements of several conditional estimates in prime number theory, assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis.

This Project Outcomes Report for the General Public is displayed verbatim as submitted by the Principal Investigator (PI) for this award. Any opinions, findings, and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this Report are those of the PI and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Science Foundation; NSF has not approved or endorsed its content. 

This grant supported research in the area of number theory. In broad terms, this research studied the distribution of the zeros of L-functions and related problems in arithmetic using tools from analytic number theory combined with ideas from harmonic analysis, Fourier analysis, automorphic forms, and algebraic number theory. The PI investigated long-standing open problems in the number theory, including questions concerning the zeros of the Riemann zeta-function and other L-functions, the zeros of polynomials, and the theory of prime numbers. Throughout the funding period, the PI conducted research in collaboration with other mathematicians, published original results in internationally recognized peer-reviewed journals, and gave numerous lectures on this research program.

Some highlights of the research carried out include using ideas from analysis to identify and in some cases solve optimization problems that arise in number theory in connection to problems such as bounding the least prime in an arithmetic progression, bounding the least quadratic non-residue, investigating the distribution of small gaps between the zeros of the Riemann zeta-function, bounding the Riemann zeta-function on the critical line, investigating the distribution of zeros of polynomials, studying Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture, and studying the distribution of low-lying zeros of L-functions in families. The PI also investigated negative moments of Riemann zeta-function, the number variance of zeros of the zeta function, and weighted distributions of the number of primes dividing an integer.

In addition to these research activities, the PI continued to mentor students (undergraduate and graduate) during the grant period. The PI supervised independent reading courses with numerous students. Two Ph.D. students and a Masters student advised by the PI graduated during this period: Meghann Moriah Lugar, Jaime Hernandez Palacios, and Jacob Derrick. The PI mentored two graduate students at other institutions, Emily Quesada-Herrera and Antonio Pedro Ramos, and published joint research with them. The PI is mentoring an undergraduate student on his honors college senior thesis, and research published with another undergraduate co-author was published in the Journal of Number Theory. 

Research during the grant period was disseminated through various journal publications, and lectures by the PI. This includes numerous invited seminar, conference, and colloquium talks given around world. Some highlights are a general audience in the PIMS Distinguished Lecture Series at the University of Lethbridge in Canada and a lecture in the Basic Notions Seminar at the International Centre for Theoretical Physics in Trieste, Italy (which has been viewed thousands of times on YouTube).

abstractText:
Skin-friction drag is responsible for energy loss for ships, aircraft, and the trucking industry. This project explores innovative methods of reducing skin-friction drag using computations and experiments. One of the promising methods for reducing skin-friction drag is to dampen wall turbulence passively using surface microstructures. While a substantial amount of effort has been made to advance wall techniques, the process is not yet completely understood. The primary aim of this project is to provide a fundamental understanding of the underlying physics of these novel surface microstructures and show that they can provide systematic control of wall turbulence to minimize skin-friction drag. The project outcomes will be disseminated to broader communities through many educational and outreach activities, such as undergraduate research programs, scientific publications, conference presentations, and summer science camps to K-12 students and teachers.

A micro airfoil structure, which is a newly proposed surface microstructure, is expected to achieve unique turbulence control capabilities due to its well-defined 3D geometry. The main objectives of the project are: (i) to demonstrate the turbulence control capability using the micro airfoil structure, (ii) to identify the connections between the control inputs created by the micro airfoil structure and the responses of skin-friction drag, (iii) to understand the fundamental mechanisms of the turbulence control and skin-friction drag reduction by the micro airfoil structure, and (iv) to recommend the optimum configurations of the single and arrays of micro airfoil structure for the maximum reduction of skin-friction drag. Direct numerical simulation and large eddy simulation will be used to compute fundamental flows, and particle image velocimetry will be used to measure velocities in the turbulent boundary layer. The fundamental knowledge obtained through this project will provide insight to answer the long-lasting questions about the dynamics of wall-bounded turbulent flows. The unique turbulence control techniques achieved by the micro airfoil structure will provide guidance to other research areas in aerospace, mechanical, chemical, and ocean engineering where turbulence control may lead to drag reduction. Project Overview: The transportation sector, encompassing shipping, aviation, and trucking, consumes over two-thirds of the oil used annually in the United States, with skin-friction drag contributing significantly to energy loss. This project aimed to diminish this drag by controlling turbulent boundary layers (TBLs) using a novel Micro Airfoil Structure (MAS). The project employed high-fidelity experimental and computational tools, including Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS), to probe the MAS’s turbulence control capabilities, elucidate underlying flow physics, optimize MAS configurations, disseminate findings, and train students in multidisciplinary research.

Intellectual Merit: The project achieved notable progress in understanding and controlling wall-bounded turbulent flows, addressing long-standing questions in fluid dynamics and turbulence research. Experimental studies, utilizing a custom-built wind tunnel and PIV, demonstrated that MAS and their arrays, fabricated via advanced additive manufacturing, can generate effective and meaningful flow control effects, such as local flow acceleration or deceleration and vortex generation, effectively modulating turbulent boundary layers. The outcomes also revealed that MAS arrays redistributed turbulent energy within the boundary layer and induced localized flow resistance that is strongly linked to skin-friction drag reduction. Computational studies, including the DNS of TBLs over MAS and other surface structures, such as riblets and superhydrophobic surfaces, led to the discovery that such surface structures or modifications can yield considerably different drag behaviors from the general understanding achieved from conventional and canonical flow situations. These computational studies also supported the experimental observations by revealing anisotropic flow structures created around MAS that may be the pivotal flow structures related to diminishing skin-friction drag of the surface. The computational efforts include one of the largest DNS simulations to date of developing TBLs over surface structures. Additionally, innovative turbulent flow analysis techniques were developed, such as the quintuple decomposition method, to isolate geometry-induced flow effects from temporal unsteadiness, enabling precise characterization of microstructure impacts. This tool revealed that collective, rather than individual, effects of surface structures drive turbulence modulation, providing guidance for their optimal array designs.

Broader Impacts: The project’s outcomes have comprehensive implications for energy efficiency and environmental sustainability. By optimizing surface microstructures to reduce SFD, the research directs the way for more efficient transportation systems, potentially lowering fuel consumption in aerospace, automotive, and marine applications. Insights gained from the studies with MAS, superhydrophobic surfaces, grooves, and riblets under non-equilibrium conditions provide performance metrics critical for developing next-generation surface modifications that can enhance fuel efficiency and reduce emissions in fluid transport systems like pipelines and HVAC ducts. Educationally, the project provided enriched training opportunities for graduate students involved, broadening their expertise in experimental and computational fluid dynamics and additive manufacturing techniques. Undergraduate courses in fluid dynamics and heat transfer incorporated project findings, connecting theoretical concepts to real-world applications. The project also created public outreach opportunities, such as Mississippi Day, where the demonstration of fluid dynamics concepts was showcased to diverse audiences. Furthermore, the simulations and experimental results have been shared with researchers worldwide through journal publications, conference presentations, and an open-access data repository. The project’s methodologies and datasets will continue to guide future research in passive flow control, fostering innovations in energy-efficient technologies. These will also support interdisciplinary applications in aerospace, mechanical, and environmental engineering.

projectOutComesReport:
The Quartz Crystal Microbalance with Dissipation (QCM-D) is an extremely sensitive balance that is primarily used to study surfaces and interfaces of materials over a wide range of areas. It detects a change in mass on a surface by monitoring the changes in frequency of the quartz crystal during operation. It determines whether the mass attached to a surface is soft or rigid by monitoring the energy loss (or ‘dissipation’) of the crystal during a change in its frequency. This state-of-the-art scientific instrument provides important information on how materials interact with each other at interfaces, and has allowed researchers at the University of Mississippi (UM) to progress their research in many areas of novel material development. Three of the key areas are:

  1. Sustainable packaging: Research in Chemical Engineering is underway to produce water-repellent paper packaging using sustainable waxes that can be easily removed from the paper after use for recycling purposes. QCM-D studies have identified several waxes which strongly attach to the cellulose surface. Some of these are easily removed upon a simple flushing process, while others are firmly attached to the paper surface. From a sustainability viewpoint, those that are more easily removed would be more suitable to reuse both the wax and the paper upon recycle. Waxes investigated to date include alkyl ketene dimer (AKD) and carnauba wax.
  2. Membrane development for water treatment: Both industry and residential communities depend on effective water treatment to negate and remove harmful contaminants. Membrane-based separation processes are widely used for their efficiency in contaminant removal, but these membranes often face challenges such as fouling during operation. To better understand these fouling mechanisms, QCM-D was employed to study the surface interactions on ion exchange membranes. Furthermore, a novel technique for creating model ion exchange membrane QCM-D sensors was developed and validated through fouling studies. The results demonstrated that the newly developed membranes effectively simulated surface interactions that occur during reversible and irreversible fouling processes.
  3. Cardiovascular health: Muscle contraction of the heart is critical in its normal functioning, and myosin II motor proteins drive the heart muscle contraction.  The QCM-D was used to investigate how myosin motors alter muscle stiffness and how this work at the molecular level scales up to facilitate contraction. Understanding the interplay between myosin and muscle contraction is necessary for understanding how muscles function normally, react to stress, and respond to drugs used to treat heart disease.

These three study areas have obvious, positive, societal impacts. Developing sustainable packaging using sustainable materials that can be recycled for re-use assists in minimizing environmental harm and use of toxic chemicals. Improvements in membrane material development promotes better water treatment methods with longer-lasting membranes. Finally, understanding the mechanisms of maintaining a healthy heart has huge implications on societal health. In all these cases, advanced knowledge was possible by studying the interfaces of connecting surfaces with the QCM-D, and has greatly assisted in overall material development and enhanced healthcare options for the future.

Besides the longer-term societal impacts expected from this work, a considerable number of students have participated in learning experiences involving the QCM-D. Two 500-level courses involving an average of approximately 15 students in each class have studied the theory and importance of surfaces/interfaces as well as participated in laboratory demonstrations. These courses are a combination of both graduate and undergraduate students, and are regularly taught in the academic curriculum. In every year of this grant, summer research programs for undergraduate students and high school students have utilized this instrument, where several students became proficient in its operation to participate in some of the studies described. As a research tool, several research groups (graduate and undergraduate students) have routinely used the QCM-D to pursue their research objectives, and write up their work in the form of posters, conference presentations, and literature articles. This state-of-the-art instrument has become a much utilized tool for material development and mechanistic research.

abstractText:
Industrial energy production processes generate gaseous products such as carbon dioxide that must be removed from the exhaust streams to meet regulatory emissions standards. The selective removal of individual molecules like carbon dioxide from enormous volumes of hot, high-pressure gas is a challenging problem. Energy-efficient separation technologies, such as membranes, are required to preserve profits and minimize environmental impacts. A special class of membranes formed from a composite of polymer and ionic liquid is a promising energy-efficient gas separation technology with demonstrated applications ranging from natural gas pretreatment to carbon emission reduction. However, polymer/ionic liquid composite membranes are not suitable for use at high pressures due to instability and performance limitations, preventing industrial deployment of these systems. This project seeks to expand the effectiveness of polymer/ionic liquid composites as gas separation membranes through an alternative design that confines the ionic liquid within a polymer platform. The resulting chemical and physical characteristics are expected to yield membranes with enhanced mechanical stability at industrially-relevant pressures and with competitive separation performance. The investigators will focus on synthesis and demonstration of polymer/ionic liquid composite membranes for selectively removing carbon dioxide from a gas stream also containing methane. Computer simulations will illustrate the fundamental mechanisms behind membrane performance, which can be used to further optimize the design. In addition to the technological benefit to society, the project will broaden the participation of underrepresented groups in STEM through hands-on undergraduate research projects. Undergraduates at the University of Mississippi will also gain awareness of the membrane science field through instructional modules developed for polymer science, membrane science, and simulation courses.

This project seeks to design a biphasic polymer/ionic liquid composite membrane with optimal gas separation properties by exploiting the beneficial changes in the ionic liquid-rich phase properties resulting from ionic liquid nano-confinement within a block copolymer platform. Through an integrated experimental and computational research approach, the investigators will elucidate the structure/property/performance relationships between block copolymer size and structure and nano-confined ionic liquid structure to develop stable gas separation membranes of industrial interest. Specifically, the design of a tunable block copolymer platform will be achieved by combining design-of-experiments methods with molecular dynamics simulations to inform experiments. The investigators hypothesize that maxima in chemical permeability and selectivity in ionic liquids exist due to scale-dependent confinement effects resulting from intramolecular ordering. The design of experiments details the use of two copolymers: polystyrene-block-poly(N, N-dimethylaminoethyl methacrylate) (PS-b-DMAEMA) and polystyrene-block-polyethylene glycol (PS-b-PEG). Two ionic liquids have been selected for study: 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)-imide [EMIM][Tf2N] and 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium thiocyanate [EMIM][SCN]. During the baseline experiments, the homopolymers of DMAEMA and polystyrene will serve as models of the hydrophilic (polar) and hydrophobic (non-polar) components of the block copolymers. Pure gas permeation of carbon dioxide and methane will be measured to assess gas separation performance of optimal biphasic membranes. Mixed permeation studies will also be conducted. Using simulations, the investigators will predict the polymer/ionic liquid interactions and quantify the nano-confinement effect on carbon dioxide and methane absorption through proper energetic and structural metrics. The investigators will work to increase student awareness of the membrane field by developing research-integrated modules for undergraduate courses in polymer science, membrane science, and molecular simulation.

Objectives and Outcomes:

Industrial plants and natural gas facilities need energy‑efficient ways to separate carbon dioxide (CO2) from methane (CH4). Traditional polymer membranes struggle at high pressures (> 20 bar) common in these operations. Our project developed a new class of “biphasic” membranes that combine block copolymers with ionic liquids (ILs), special salts that stay liquid at room temperature instead of turning into solid crystals, and strategically “nanoconfine” the IL phase inside the copolymer. This concept uses the copolymer to provide mechanical strength, while the nanoconfined IL provides highly selective transport for CO2, so the membrane is both robust and high-performing.

Across the life of the award, we pursued a tightly integrated experimental/computational program. We designed and cast block copolymer/IL membranes (using polystyrene (PS)-b-polyethylene oxide (PEO) and PS-b-2-(dimethylamino)ethyl methacrylate (DMAEMA) frameworks) and measured mixed‑gas permeation of CO2/CH4, while parallel simulations probed how nanoconfinement at the polymer/IL interfaces modifies gas solubility and transport. Our work showed that lamellar and cylindrical microstructures in these systems are frequently optimal because they keep the IL in place under pressure while creating efficient pathways for CO2 transport. Our molecular and mesoscopic simulations revealed why these membranes perform well. When the IL forms a thin, nanoconfined layer between polymer domains, CO2 dissolves and diffuses more readily than CH4, boosting overall separation. In direct comparisons to bulk (unconfined) IL, CO2/CH4 permselectivity increases on average by about 40-50%, with the most favorable cases reaching roughly three‑fold improvement at a 5‑nm confinement length. These findings identify interfacial regions as active sites for selective CO2 uptake and suggest a practical design rule, i.e., tune the confinement length and morphology to hit a “sweet spot” in selectivity before behavior returns toward bulk IL.

We also advanced understanding of pressure stability. By building membranes in which the IL is embedded within continuous polymer phases, we addressed a long‑standing problem with supported IL membranes, i.e., IL displacement under elevated transmembrane pressures. The biphasic block copolymer platform was devised specifically to achieve robustness at industrial‑relevant pressures (> 5 bar), while maintaining competitive CO2/CH4 performance.

 

Key Outputs:

  • Published findings on IL nanoconfinement and gas transport in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF)-confined IL significantly improved CO2/CH4 selectivity over bulk IL.
  • Published mesoscopic morphology mapping in Macromolecules: Self‑assembled PS‑b‑PEO/IL membrane morphologies were characterized across IL loadings and copolymer block size ratios.
  • Published mechanism‑level confirmation of IL nanoconfinement effects on CO2/CH4 separation: Combined mesoscopic dynamics and hybrid GCMC‑MD simulations demonstrated nanoconfining IL between polymer phases enhances CO2 solubility and transport, yielding substantially higher CO2/CH4 permselectivity than bulk ILs, pointing to optimal confinement lengths near 5 nm.
  • Dissemination of results in the Annual Meeting of the American Institute of Chemical Engineers (AIChE) in 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2025.

 

Societal/Economic Benefits:

Separating CO2 more efficiently can lower the energy cost and greenhouse gas footprint of natural gas processing and other industrial separations. By demonstrating stable and tunable copolymer/IL membranes designed around the physical chemistry principles of IL nanoconfinement, this project creates pathways to membranes that are both durable at higher pressures and more selective. These benefits translate into lower operating costs, reduced emissions, and easier retrofits to existing units.

 

Intellectual Merit:

This work answers a central question in membrane science: Can confining an IL at the nanoscale make it both more selective and stable? Our results say yes. By connecting morphology (how phases arrange themselves), interfacial physics (how IL and polymer interact), and transport (how CO2 and CH4 move and dissolve), we established structure-property-performance rules that guide the design of next‑generation membranes. The combined experimental measurements and simulations, spanning phase diagrams, interfacial ordering, and mixed‑gas transport, provide a mechanistic foundation for engineering IL‑based membranes for gas separations at elevated pressures.

 

Broader Impacts:

The project engaged four undergraduate and two graduate students (one female), in hands‑on research experiences in membrane science and molecular simulation. We developed course modules integrated into a chemical engineering elective course (Ch E 550 - Membrane Science and Engineering), benefitting on average 10 students at both undergraduate and graduate levels on a bi-annual basis. We also developed a membrane formation demonstration for middle school and high school students. This hands-on activity was conducted for approximately 75 students in partnership with the NanoEngineering REU housed within University of Mississippi’s Biomedical Engineering Department. These activities broadened awareness of separation science, provided real‑world teamwork and data analysis experience, and enriched our curriculum with research‑based content.

 

Future Prospects:

Our findings point to practical design factors such as copolymer block size ratio, IL loading, and confinement length, that manufacturers can use to tailor membranes for specific gas streams. Overall, our findings inform industrial membrane design for natural gas upgrading and carbon capture. Future steps could include scaling membrane fabrication, long‑duration stability tests under industry operating conditions, and exploring other IL/polymer pairs to broaden applicability to CO2/N2 and sour‑gas separations.

In this project, funded by the Chemical Structure, Dynamics & Mechanisms B Program of the Chemistry Division, Professors Jared Delcamp and Nathan Hammer of the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry at the University of Mississippi are developing new classes of organic dye molecules that exhibit interesting light-matter interactions. The goal of this research is to design organic dyes that absorb low-energy light to enable the design of higher-performing electronic devices such as night vision technologies, infrared cameras, secure display technologies, solar cells including transparent ones integrable with buildings, solar batteries, and artificial photosynthetic systems. This project relies on interdisciplinary research utilizing organic, inorganic, materials, and physical chemistry.  To encourage STEM involvement, outreach activities to the general public and student groups with large populations of underrepresented minorities are planned. A yearly summer research program brings STEM students onto campus to conduct independent research related to this award. 

Near-infrared absorbing organic dyes capable of undergoing interfacial charge separation at metal oxide interfaces are needed to advance a number of emerging technologies. Metal oxide bound organic dyes that absorb low energy photons (>800 nm) and subsequently undergo charge separation in high quantum yields are rare. Systems in these regions are often limited in utility by excited-state and charge separated state lifetimes. The study of fundamental physical organic chemistry is needed to enable the rational design of systems using low energy photons. In this project, four types of systems are studied at interfaces: (1) dyes with delocalized charge states after electron transfer to metal oxides, (2) dyes with excited-state aromaticity for prolonging excited states to promote higher quantum yields of interfacial photoinduced charge separation, (3) double cross-conjugated dyes for lower energy photon absorptions, and (4) Near-infrared absorbing chromophores incorporating proaromatic functionality.

projectOutComesReport:
Designing strategies to effectively use low energy photons (>800 nm) with organic optoelectronic materials is a critical challenge with substantial transformative capacity. Specifically, photoinduced charge separation at metal oxide-organic molecule interfaces using near-infrared (NIR) photons is an area which could have tremendous impact on solar cells, solar batteries, night vision technologies, NIR cameras, photosensors, and photoelectrochemical cells including artificial photosynthesis systems. The goal of this research program was to use physical organic chemistry concepts to rationally design deeper NIR absorbing organic materials with precisely controlled energetics for low energy photon conversion to charge separated states across organic dye-MO interfaces.

Intellectual Merit: A total of sixteen new designer dyes were discovered during the project period that can convert >800 nm photons to electric potentials. Many of these dyes exhibit good quantum yields (≥70%) when used with TiO2. These results were disseminated in a total of eleven peer-reviewed publications that credit this award. One accomplishment includes discovering the highest photocurrent generating squaraine dyes known in the literature. Charge separation durations at 0.1 s using the squaraine dyes in functional dye sensitized solar cells that produced electricity beyond 900 nm was demonstrated. This result is exceptional at TiO2 and exceeded the project target of 0.01 s. This long-lived charge separation is likely the direct result of proaromatic behavior, which was engineered into many of the dyes. This award supports the participation of undergraduate students, graduate students, and postdoctoral students at the Annual National Organization for the Professional Advancement of Black Chemists and Chemical Engineers (NOBCChE) conference, held Sept. 24-25, 2020. The 2020 NOBCChE conference is in a virtual format in 2020 due to disruptions from COVID-19. Selected participants are from underrepresented minority groups in the Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) fields. In addition to providing registration support for students, this award enables the development of a robust online platform for participant engagement. This is funded by Divisions of Chemistry and Materials Research, both of the Mathematical and Physical Sciences Directorate, the Division of Molecular and Cellular Biosciences in the Biological Science Directorate, and the Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, and Transport Systems as well as the Division of Industrial Innovation and Partnerships, both of the Engineering Directorate. The Principle Investigator is Godfrey Murrell of the University of Mississippi. 

This award provides opportunities for participants to engage in four major areas of focus: 1) STEM technical and professional development; 2) networking and mentorship opportunities with STEM professionals; 3) exposure to prestigious minority role models in STEM; and 4) STEM career advancement opportunities. Student participants interact with peers and professionals from industry, government, and academia to develop collaborations and to explore opportunities to pursue graduate degrees in the chemistry, chemical engineering and related disciplines. This is accomplished through a virtual conference. These opportunities not only impact these specific participating individuals, but also benefit the larger community of STEM field practitioners as these activities are useful in recruiting and retaining individuals from underrepresented talent pools. NOBCChE seeks to increase the number of minorities in the STEM workforce. The compression of the typical weeklong NOBCChE conference to two days is augmented by post conference access to various materials. Assessment plans enable the comparison of prior in person NOBCChE events to this first ever virtual event.

Accomplishments

* What are the major goals of the project?

The mission of NOBCChE is to build an eminent cadre of people of color in science and technology. NOBCChE fulfills part of its mission through local, regional, national and global programs that assist the membership in fully realizing their capabilities and potential in academic, professional, and entrepreneurial pursuits in chemistry, chemical engineering, and STEM-related fields. The NOBCChE Annual Conferences brought together, in one setting, underrepresented minority-serving institutions (HBCUs and HSIs), Majority (Research) Institutions, key federal agencies, and industries committed to increasing the number of underrepresented minorities, including women and those with disabilities, representation in chemistry, chemical engineering, and STEM-related careers. In particular, the 2020 NOBCChE conference focused on creating a pathway to STEM careers by identifying and sponsoring 200 underrepresented minority students, including women and persons with disabilities in chemistry, chemical engineering, and related STEM fields to attend the conference virtually.

 

The meeting was designed to provide young researchers a platform to present research and receive feedback (ConneXions Poster Session), showcase the research of scientist regarded as experts in their respective fields (Master Scientist Sessions), and provide a space for discussion to foster partnership and collaboration that can lead to new research, innovations, and solutions to global challenges (DuPont GOLD Competition).

  • Presented the Master Scientist Sessions featuring the Percy Julian and Winifred Burks-Houck Lectures.
  • Held more than 20 post-conference talks.

Specific Objectives:

  • To have more than 200 underrepresented students participate in learning, speaking and discussions during the virtual conference and post-conference activities
  • To present more than 50 training and professional development opportunities

  • A total of 420 minority students participated in the virtual conference and the post-conference activities including 282 graduate and 112 undergraduate students.  54 percent were female. 
  • 53 workshops, talks and other professional development training opportunities were presented.

More information on student outcomes for the conference (webinars and on-demand sessions) is in the attached external evaluation report.

abstractText:
Organizational success is often attributed to the elite group of executives atop an organization and their ability to guide the organization into an uncertain future. However, developing and implementing strategy typically requires many members of both upper and middle management to communicate and shape strategy through formal (top-down) and/or informal (lateral, upward) processes of influence. Unfortunately, the patterns of communication and informal influence that often arise among upper- and middle-level management groups can pose problems for strategic effectiveness. Such leadership failures are common, costly, and cannot be addressed without a better understanding of who will lead and who will follow in the upper layers of organizations. Although prior research has examined the characteristics of top executives to understand firm effectiveness, scholars agree that how top managers and middle-level managers need to interact to propel their firms toward greater success remains a ?black box'. This project delves into this black box by advancing and testing new theory related to the multilevel causes and consequences of the networked patterns of leadership and communication processes that emerge in the upper levels of organizations. By studying the complex dynamics inherent in the leadership of large organizations, this project directly and positively impacts each participating organization as well as the aggregate economy that relies on these organizations. 

This project leverages partnerships with the Center for Creative Leadership (CCL) and the Gutierrez Energy Management Institute (GEMI) in order to conduct survey- and interview-based research with upper- and middle-level managers from approximately 50-75 organizations from a variety of industries (Study 1) and approximately 25 organizations within the Energy Industry -- an industry that is vital to national interests (Study 2). As a recruitment incentive, our research team is providing tailored feedback for each participating organization in the form of an hour-long virtual debrief presentation and personalized report delivered to senior executives. To maximize internal validity, field study results are being combined with a large-scale controlled laboratory experiment manipulating the drivers of leadership and communication networks in hierarchical multi-group systems (Study 3). Therefore, this research program connects micro-, meso-, and macro-level organizational theories and corresponding research methods in order to address critical and unanswered questions related to the drivers and outcomes of informal leadership and communication networks in the upper levels of organizations.

projectOutComesReport:
Traditionally, organizational success has been attributed mainly to senior executives. However, emerging research highlights the crucial role of middle managers in both strategy development and implementation. Indeed, effective strategy often relies on a strategic leadership system of upper and middle managers influencing each other through both formal and informal relationships. Unfortunately, the networked patterns of leadership and communication that often emerge among members of strategic leadership systems can sometimes hinder strategic effectiveness. For instance, senior leaders may disregard influence attempts by middle managers and managers from different subunits may prioritize their own goals over those of the organization, creating conflict and misalignment. These leadership failures are common and costly, and addressing them requires a deeper understanding of who leads and who follows within strategic leadership systems. 

This research project advanced understanding of why networks of informal leadership and communication develop among senior- and middle-level managers, as well as the implications of these networks. Specifically, this project connected micro-, meso-, and macro-level organizational theories and research methods to identify: (1) the drivers (antecedents) of informal leadership and communication networks within strategic leadership systems; (2) the individual and group outcomes associated with these networks; and (3) the practical implications of revealing network patterns and their antecedents to organizational leaders. We addressed these questions by collaborating with over 1060 participants comprising 16 strategic leadership systems. We conducted additional research in leadership development training contexts, classroom settings, and virtual computational modeling environments to extend the robustness of our findings. 

Network Antecedents: Our results emphasize that formal structures do not fully explain informal leadership structures. Although formal reporting lines, authority hierarchies, and team memberships provide an essential framework, leadership relationships are often shaped by additional factors. Specifically, individual differences such as personality traits, gender, shared priorities, and various forms of interpersonal similarity play a critical role in determining who emerges as an informal leader. Personality fit with specific leaders and congruence between individual and organizational priorities further influence the development of these relationships. These factors often explain the informal connections that emerge alongside formal systems, offering a more nuanced understanding of how leadership operates in practice. For example, we found that even within hierarchical organizations, middle managers frequently exert informal influence on senior leaders, particularly in contexts requiring rapid decision-making or specialized expertise. Similarly, lateral influence among peers is often driven by shared experiences or professional goals, transcending the boundaries of formal subunit divisions. These findings underscore the complexity of leadership dynamics, highlighting that leadership is not confined to formal authority or positional power.

Network Outcomes: Our research demonstrates that informal leadership and communication networks significantly impact key organizational outcomes. These networks can play critical roles in facilitating strategic consensus and preventing the pitfalls of fragmentation or isolated echo chambers. For example, when informal networks are robust and interconnected, they facilitate alignment across leadership tiers, enabling organizations to coalesce around shared objectives. In contrast, fragmented networks can lead to miscommunication, competing priorities, and strategic misalignment. Furthermore, informal networks have important implications for organizational resilience during periods of disruption, such as the COVID-19 pandemic. At the team level, network patterns can influence team performance and assembly dynamics. At the individual level, they shape career trajectories, determining who gains access to critical developmental opportunities and whose voices carry influence within the organization.

Practical Implications: The project’s findings were enthusiastically received by the senior leaders with whom we collaborated. Over the course of numerous debriefs, leaders expressed overwhelmingly positive reactions to gaining insights into their leadership and communication networks. The visualization and analysis of these patterns provided actionable information about influence flows, bottlenecks, and disconnects within their strategic leadership systems. Leaders frequently took proactive measures to address miscommunications and bridge gaps, leveraging the insights to realign teams and strengthen organizational cohesion. For example, leaders reported using the findings from the analysis to identify who to tap into for key roles in change initiatives, who to support to more freely share their knowledge with others, and where to build communication bridges.

In summary, this project revealed that informal leadership and communication networks are critical to the functioning of strategic leadership systems, shaping strategic consensus, team performance, and individual career success. Investigating these networks can also provide senior leaders with powerful tools for diagnosing and addressing organizational misalignments. The findings emphasize the need for organizations to look beyond formal structures and invest in understanding the informal dynamics that underpin effective leadership to enhance strategic alignment, resilience, and long-term success. By bridging and extending the complementary literatures of strategic management, leadership emergence, and team collaboration, this project delved into the “black box” of the interpersonal processes involved in strategy development and implementation. We found that informal networks are as vital as formal structures for achieving strategic objectives, offering a comprehensive understanding of how leadership networks influence organizational outcomes.
